text.p: Following are some of the leading stories in the Swedish papers this morning. Reuters has not verified these stories and does not vouch for their accuracy.
- Swedes with immigrant backgrounds are clearly under-represented in local politics, a survey shows.

- The sale of Incentive AB's stake in ABB AB for 12.4 billion crowns, of which half was bought by investment group AB Investor, clarifies the complex ownership structure of Swedish-Swiss electrical engineering company ABB.
- The National Labour Board Ams will step up its fight against illegal employment of construction workers. The unions welcome such a move.
- Gross Domestic Product rose 1.6 percent in the first quarter of the year compared to the year earlier period, making for a weak economic start for the year.

- Sweden's powerful financers, the Wallenbergs, are reshuffling their large stakes with investment and medical technology group Incentive, selling half its stake in ABB AB, partly to investment company Investor. Both groups are part of the Wallenberg family's financial empire. ABB AB is the Swedish parent company of Swiss-Swedish engineer ABB.

- The new wealth tax does not only cause family-controlled groups to flee from the bourse's main A list to the smaller O list, it could also cause futures and derivatives trader OM Gruppen to lose a large part of its private customers to banks and brokerages.
The new tax only concerns listed options and futures, which in Sweden are traded by OM, while tailored options and futures, OTC derivatives, handled by banks and brokerages are exempt from tax.

- He strikes again -- for the second time in a short period the managing director of investment and medical technology group Incentive AB, Mikael Lilius, carries out a multi-billion crown deal. This time he sold half the group's stake in ABB AB for 12.4 billion crowns. The deal restores Incentive's financial strength to what it was before the purchase of U.S. dialysis clinics group Vivra.
- Furniture chain IKEA plans to boost its annual investments by about 50 percent or by 9.3 billion crowns over three years with a focus on Asia.

- The European Commission says the fact that it expressed serious doubts about the proposed cross-channel traffic cooperation between Sweden's Stena Line AB and P&O does not mean it won't give the two companies clearance to form the the joint venture.

- Medical technology company Q-Med plans to seek a listing on the Stockholm Stock Exchange within a year. The company markets a substance which is said to eliminate wrinkles when injected under the skin. Clinical tests of the chemical, called Restylane, are due to begin later this year for its use as a substitute for silicon breast implants.
